title: Simple cyclic tag systems show random fluctuations in sequence growth

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Simple cyclic tag systems show random fluctuations in sequence growth

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Some cyclic tag systems with two alternating blocks, started from a single black element, produce sequences whose average growth is steady but whose fluctuations about that growth are in many respects random.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: if one looks at the fluctuations in this growth, as in the plots on the next page, then one finds that these fluctuations are in many respects random.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 3, “The World of Simple Programs”; section “Cyclic Tag Systems” (from p. 95), p. 95. Scope: cyclic tag systems with two blocks

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch03-14: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Exact arbitrarily long trajectories are inexpensive to generate and standard time-series tests directly assess the stated fluctuation properties. The claim is about random-like statistics rather than true stochasticity, making finite operational resolution reasonable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Run the specified two-block cyclic tag systems from one black element, estimate the growth trend, and subject detrended increments to autocorrelation, spectral, distributional, and compression tests. Passing prespecified random-like criteria supports the claim; strong regular dependence refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Deterministic fluctuations may pass finite randomness tests while retaining hidden structure.

Random in many respects does not identify a unique test battery.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The systems are particular two-block cyclic tag rules, and their length sequences are ordinary string rewriting. Detrending by the stated average growth and applying a public test suite confirms or challenges the randomness clause for those examples. Because the claim says 'some' systems and 'many respects,' a single well-tested example carries the existential reading, with the usual limit of statistical tests.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Simulate the published two-block cyclic tag systems from a single black element, subtract a linear trend of one half element per step, and run randomness tests on the residuals. The claim is confirmed if at least some of those systems pass, and refuted if every such system has periodic or otherwise plainly structured fluctuations.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The trend of one half element per step should be fixed from the rule, not fit so as to whiten the residuals.

In many respects random is relative to the test list; passing a battery does not prove randomness.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Among two-block cyclic tag systems started from a single black element, at least one produces a sequence whose length grows at a steady linear rate while the fluctuations about that growth behave like a random walk (unbounded, diffusive scaling) and the leading-element sequence that drives them is incompressible to a substantial degree.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py enumerates the 225 rules, stores each history as one growing tape (sequence at step t is tape[t:]), screens all rules for 100,000 steps, then runs the 80 growing rules for 1,000,000 steps. For each it fits L(t) linearly, computes local growth rates in 10 windows, estimates the Hurst exponent of the detrended residual from the variance of increments at lags 1..8192, and lzma-compresses the packed leading-element bit sequence. Two seeded control sequences (i.i.d. Bernoulli(3/4); first-order Markov with no '00' and P(1)=3/4, the local statistics Wolfram reports for example (d)) calibrate the compression measure. Per-rule results are in derived/systems.csv.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Family: all 225 cyclic tag systems with two blocks, each block a binary string of length 0-3 (15 choices per block), initial sequence {1}, Wolfram's update (remove first element; if it was 1 append the current block; blocks alternate every step). Stage 1: run each system 100,000 steps; a system is 'growing' if the sequence never empties and its final length is >= 1000. Stage 2: run each growing system 1,000,000 steps and compute (i) linear fit of length L(t) vs t: R^2 >= 0.999 and local growth rates over 10 equal windows all within 25% of the global slope ('steady growth'); (ii) Hurst exponent H of the detrended residual r(t) = L(t) - (a + b t), estimated as half the log-log slope of Var[r(t+tau) - r(t)] over tau = 2^0..2^13, in [0.35, 0.65] ('random-walk-like fluctuations'); (iii) lzma (preset 9 | EXTREME) compressed size of the packed leading-element bit sequence >= 0.25 bits per symbol ('incompressible driver'). The claim PASSES if at least one system satisfies (i), (ii) and (iii) simultaneously. Secondary, reported but not decisive: whether the book's own examples (d) {{1},{1,0,1}} and (e) {{1,1,1},{0}} pass.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if no system in the 225-member family satisfies all of (i)-(iii): i.e. every growing system has either unsteady growth, bounded or non-diffusive fluctuations (H outside [0.35, 0.65]), or a leading-element sequence that compresses below 0.25 bits per symbol (periodic or nested).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: systems passing all three pre-registered criteria

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Wolfram's 'fluctuations in this growth ... are in many respects random' (p. 95-96) is read as: fluctuations about the mean growth are unbounded and scale diffusively like a random walk (Hurst exponent near 1/2), and the binary sequence of leading elements, which fully determines the growth, cannot be compressed to a small fraction of its length (so it is neither periodic nor nested, in contrast to the book's example (c), whose leading column is a nested Sturmian sequence). 'Steady growth' is read as a linear fit with R^2 >= 0.999 and stable local rates. The family is the smallest natural family containing the book's examples (d) and (e). This is a computational test; no external data is needed.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Two-block cyclic tag systems with blocks of length 0-3 (generated by analysis.py)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
By the letter of the pre-registration the composite test fails: 0 of 225 systems pass all three criteria, because no growing system compresses to more than 0.115 bits per symbol (criterion iii). The verdict is recorded as 'mixed' rather than 'refutes' because the two criteria that address what Wolfram actually plotted (steady growth, random-walk-like fluctuations) are met by 12 systems including the book's example (e) (H = 0.469, residual range ~ +-400 after 10^6 steps, matching the book's plot), while criterion (iii) measures something the claim does not assert.

Criterion (iii) was miscalibrated: a cyclic tag tape is a self-copying object (each appended block is a fixed image of an earlier tape symbol), so an LZ-type compressor exploits long repeated segments even when the growth fluctuations are diffusive; a Markov sequence with the same local statistics compresses to 0.73 bits/symbol, the real tapes to 0.06-0.12. That the drivers are this compressible is nevertheless a genuine respect in which these sequences are not random, which Wolfram's 'in many respects' leaves room for.

The book's example (d) {{1},{1,0,1}} has H = 0.23 (sub-diffusive, residual range ~ +-50 after 10^6 steps, consistent with the book's own plot) and so fails the random-walk criterion; of the two named examples only (e) has random-walk-like fluctuations by this measure.

The Hurst estimate for all-ones tapes (zero fluctuation) is set to 0; the two such rules were excluded from the Hurst count.

Finite-run statistics cannot establish randomness; the test can only fail to find regularity at the scales examined (lags up to 8192, 10^6 steps).
